tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: DeferredToolPlaceholder
tools.description: Reserved placeholder that keeps deferred tool loading active; never call this tool.

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to write (must be absolute, not relative)

content.description: The content to write to the file

content.text:
<system-reminder>
Codebase and user instructions are shown below. Be sure to adhere to these instructions. IMPORTANT: These instructions OVERRIDE any default behavior and you MUST follow them exactly as written.

Contents of c:\Users\thema\OneDrive\Desktop\Project2\project2-harness2\project2-harness2\CLAUDE.md (project instructions, checked into the codebase):

@AGENTS.md

Contents of c:\Users\thema\OneDrive\Desktop\Project2\project2-harness2\project2-harness2\AGENTS.md (project instructions, checked into the codebase):

# AGENTS.md: Project 2 context for all agents

Every agent (builder, reviewer, tester) reads this file first.

## Project goal

Classify Android apps as malware or goodware from their API-call features, and find a sustainable approach that stays accurate as the data drifts over 8 years (2014-2021). The full assignment is in ASSIGNMENT.md.

## Dataset

- Location: input_data/ (not committed to git).
- 16 CSV files named sampled_<YEAR>_<CLASS>_api.csv, e.g. sampled_2017_malware_api.csv. YEAR is 2014-2021. CLASS is "malware" or "benign" (benign = goodware). One malware file and one benign file per year.
- Year and class come ONLY from the file name. Parse them with a regex; fail loudly on a name that does not match.
- Columns: every file has 1,849 columns. The first column is "apkname" (package name + hash, an identifier). It must be dropped; the other 1,848 columns are API-call features (column names are Dalvik method signatures). All files have the same columns in the same order.
- Rows: ASSIGNMENT.md says 1,500 rows per file, but the real files differ: 2014-2018 files have 9,000 rows each; 2019-2021 files have 1,500 rows each. Code must not assume a fixed row count; it must check 1,849 columns and report the actual row counts.
- Label: target column "label", 1 = malware, 0 = goodware (benign).
- Feature values: non-negative integer call counts, heavy-tailed (max around 92,000). No missing values. Roughly 850-1,125 columns are all-zero within any single file. The 2014-2018 files contain many duplicate rows and repeated apknames; keep them unless PLAN.md justifies otherwise, and report them.
- Memory: the combined data is about 100,000 x 1,848. Load features as int32 or float32, not int64.

## Folder layout

- src/: project code (builder only).
- tests/: pytest tests test_stepN_*.py and test logs stepN_test_log.md (tester only; the student adds failure decisions).
- docs/: one builder report per step.
- reviews/: one review report per step (reviewer writes comments; student writes the decision log).
- results/: CSV and Markdown result tables (and optional PNG figures) written by the code.
- transcripts/: saved agent sessions (saved by the harness; agents never edit these).
- PLAN.md: the plan for Steps 1-7. README.md, REPORT.md and REFLECTION.md: written by the student.

## Coding conventions

- Python 3, pandas, numpy, scikit-learn, scipy. matplotlib is allowed for figures (add it to requirements.txt). No other libraries without asking.
- One module per concern in src/ (e.g. data.py, drift.py, preprocess.py, models.py, evaluate.py, sustainable.py) plus src/main.py as the entry point.

content.content:
1	# PLAN.md: Project 2 plan (Steps 1-7)
2	
3	Author: builder agent. Status: initial version (Step 0), before review.
4	Data facts used here come from AGENTS.md. Nothing in this plan has been run yet; no result is claimed.
5	
6	## 0. Global decisions
7	
8	### Train/test split by year
9	
10	| Role | Years | Use |
11	|---|---|---|
12	| Train | 2014, 2015, 2016 | fit preprocessing and models |
13	| Tuning (only if needed) | train on 2014-2015, validate on 2016 | choose hyperparameters; then refit on 2014-2016 |
14	| Test | 2017, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021 | evaluation only; every metric is reported pooled AND per year |
15	
16	### How leakage between years is prevented
17	
18	1. One function `check_no_overlap(train_years, test_years)` (in `src/preprocess.py`) raises `ValueError` if either set is empty, if the sets intersect, or if `max(train_years) >= min(test_years)` (training years must all precede test years). Every train/predict call in Steps 3-7 goes through it.
19	   - **Exemption (Step 2).** `concept_drift_matrix` in `src/drift.py` is diagnostic: it fits a scaler and a model on each single year (including 2017-2021) and predicts other years, so it does not obey the train-2014-2016 rule or `check_no_overlap`. Nothing it produces feeds Steps 3-7 (no features, hyperparameters or split choices). The leakage tests skip `drift.py`; they apply to Steps 3-7 only.
20	2. Every fitted object (zero-column mask, `StandardScaler`, classifiers) is fit on the training rows only. Test rows are only passed to `transform` / `predict`. `log1p` is stateless, so it cannot leak.
21	3. Tuning never touches 2017-2021.
22	4. Step 7: year t is predicted before it is used for training (see Step 7). Expanding/sliding windows refit preprocessing on the window only.
23	5. Cross-year duplicates: the 2014-2018 files have many duplicate rows and repeated apknames. Step 1 reports (a) exact duplicate feature rows within a year and (b) apknames or identical feature vectors shared between a training year and a test year. I keep all rows by default (AGENTS.md); no rows are removed from the main results. Step 1 reports, per test year, the count and share of test rows whose exact feature vector also occurs in the training years (2014-2016). Steps 5 and 6 add a sensitivity row (`subset = "no_train_duplicate"`) with metrics on only the test rows that have no exact duplicate in the training years, and state in the report how many test rows were excluded.
24	6. Step 2 (KS tests, accuracy matrix) is descriptive. Its output is never used to select features, hyperparameters or the split.
25	
26	### Conventions (from AGENTS.md)
27	random_state=42; features as float32/int32; pathlib paths relative to the repo root; docstrings and type hints on every function; one module per concern; cache in the git-ignored `cache/` folder (see `load_all` in Step 1 for the cache rules); small commits tagged `[builder]`.
28	
29	### Shared constants (`src/config.py`)
30	`ROOT`, `DATA_DIR`, `RESULTS_DIR`, `DOCS_DIR`, `SEED = 42`, `MIN_SUPPORT = 10`, `CACHE_DIR`, `CACHE_SCHEMA_VERSION`, `TRAIN_YEARS = (2014, 2015, 2016)`, `TEST_YEARS = (2017, ..., 2021)`, `TUNE_TRAIN_YEARS = (2014, 2015)`, `TUNE_VAL_YEAR = 2016`, `N_RAW_COLUMNS = 1849`, `LABEL_COL = "label"`, `YEAR_COL = "year"`.
31	
32	### Entry point (`src/main.py`)
33	`main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> int`. `python -m src.main` runs Steps 1-7 in order; `--step N` (1-7) runs one step (running it first runs any earlier step it needs, using the cache). Prints a short summary, writes `results/`. Target: under about 15 minutes in total (see runtime notes per step).
34	
35	---
36	
37	## Changes after review
38	
39	Source: `reviews/step0_plan_review.md` (Decision log). Comment 10 was Rejected and is not applied.
40	
41	| Comment | Change in PLAN.md |
42	|---|---|
43	| 1 | SGD no longer uses `class_weight` (rejected by `partial_fit`); test must call `partial_fit` on `build_model("sgd")`. |
44	| 2 | Section 0: explicit exemption; `concept_drift_matrix` fits on single years, leakage tests skip `drift.py`. |
45	| 3 | `MIN_SUPPORT = 10`: keep columns non-zero in at least 10 training rows; documented in step 3 report; near-constant column test. |
46	| 4 | Step 1 reports test rows duplicated in 2014-2016 (`train_duplicate_mask`); Steps 5 and 6 add a no-duplicate sensitivity row; main results keep all rows. |
47	| 5 | `check_no_overlap` also requires `max(train_years) < min(test_years)`; Step 2 matrix exempt. |
48	| 6 | Cache keyed on file names, sizes, mtimes and schema version; column names stored; schema checks rerun on load; stored in git-ignored `cache/`. |
49	| 7 | `train_all_from_split` moved into the Step 4 function list; Step 7 guard is `window_years` plus `check_no_overlap`. |
50	| 8 | Step 7 report notes the row-count imbalance and lists each window's year composition. No equal-rows variant. |
51	| 9 | Step 2 report caveat: duplicates and ties inflate KS p-values; effect size is the main signal. |
52	| 11 | `list_data_files` runs `parse_filename` on every CSV so stray files raise; stray-file test added. |
53	
54	---
55	
56	## Step 1: Prepare the data (`src/data.py`)
57	
58	**Approach.** Read the 16 CSVs, take year and class only from the file name, drop `apkname`, add `label` (malware=1, benign=0) and `year`, validate the schema, and combine.
59	
60	**Functions.**
61	- `parse_filename(name: str) -> tuple[int, int]`: regex `^sampled_(\d{4})_(malware|benign)_api\.csv$` on the base name; returns `(year, label)`. Raises `ValueError` on any other name, a year outside 2014-2021, or a bad class.
62	- `list_data_files(data_dir: Path = DATA_DIR) -> list[Path]`: lists every `*.csv` in `data_dir` and runs `parse_filename` on each, so a stray or misnamed CSV raises `ValueError` (not ignored). Returns the sorted list; also raises if there is not exactly one malware and one benign file for each of 2014-2021 (16 files).
63	- `load_file(path: Path) -> pd.DataFrame`: reads the CSV, checks the shape is `(n, 1849)` and the first column is `apkname`, drops it, casts the 1,848 features to int32, appends `label` (int8) and `year` (int16) from `parse_filename`. Raises `ValueError` if the column count is not 1,849 or any value is negative or missing. Does not assert a row count.
64	- `read_apknames(path: Path) -> pd.Series`: the `apkname` column only (for the duplicate/overlap audit; never used as a feature).
65	- `load_year(year: int, data_dir: Path = DATA_DIR) -> pd.DataFrame`: concatenates that year's malware and benign files.
66	- `validate_feature_order(frames: list[pd.DataFrame]) -> None`: raises if any frame's feature columns differ from the first one in names or order.
67	- `combine_years(frames: dict[int, pd.DataFrame]) -> pd.DataFrame`: concatenates years in order (calls `validate_feature_order`); `ignore_index=True`.
68	- `load_all(data_dir: Path = DATA_DIR, use_cache: bool = True) -> pd.DataFrame`: the whole dataset (~100,000 x 1,850 incl. label, year). Cache rules: stored in `cache/` (git-ignored; `CACHE_DIR` in `src/config.py`). The cache key is a hash of each CSV's file name, size and mtime plus `CACHE_SCHEMA_VERSION` (a constant bumped whenever `src/data.py` changes how data is built). The cache file holds the feature column names with the arrays; on every cache load the schema checks run again (1,848 feature columns in the stored order, `label`/`year` present, no negatives). A key mismatch or failed check rebuilds from the CSVs. If this proves complicated, the cache is dropped rather than weakened.
69	- `cache_key(data_dir: Path) -> str`: the hash described above (used by `load_all`).
70	- `feature_columns(df: pd.DataFrame) -> list[str]`: all columns except `label` and `year` (1,848 names).
71	- `summarize_data(df: pd.DataFrame, data_dir: Path = DATA_DIR) -> pd.DataFrame`: one row per year: files loaded, rows, feature columns, malware count, benign count, exact duplicate rows, all-zero feature columns, apknames repeated within the year, and the number of rows in the year whose feature vector also occurs in an earlier year, and (test years) the number and share of rows whose feature vector occurs in 2014-2016.
72	- `train_duplicate_mask(df: pd.DataFrame, train_years=TRAIN_YEARS) -> np.ndarray`: boolean mask over all rows of `df`, True where the row's exact feature vector also occurs in a training-year row (for training-year rows themselves it is not used). Used by Steps 1, 5 and 6.
73	- `write_data_summary(summary: pd.DataFrame, path: Path) -> None`: Markdown + CSV.
74	
75	**Report.** `docs/step1_data_summary.md`: files per year, real row counts (not 1,500), 1,849 raw columns and 1,848 features after dropping `apkname`, malware/benign counts per year, duplicate/overlap audit, dtype and memory use. Table also saved to `results/step1_data_summary.csv`.
76	
77	**Testing.** Synthetic CSVs in `tmp_path`: `parse_filename` accepts valid names and rejects bad ones (wrong year, wrong class, extra suffix, path with directories); `load_file` drops the first column, gives 1,848 features, correct label from name, wrong column count raises; mismatched feature order raises; `combine_years` row count equals the sum of inputs; label and year columns are right. `list_data_files` raises on a stray CSV (e.g. `notes.csv`) in the folder and on a missing or duplicated year/class file. Cache: `cache_key` changes when a file's size or mtime changes or the schema version changes; a second `load_all` returns an equal frame; touching a CSV forces a rebuild; a cache with altered column names or order is rejected. Integration test (skipped if `input_data/` is absent): 16 files, 1,849 raw columns each, 18,000 rows per year for 2014-2018 and 3,000 for 2019-2021, equal malware and benign counts, no NaN.
78	
79	---
80	
81	## Step 2: Handle data drift (`src/drift.py`)
82	
83	**Approach.** Measure feature drift with the two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, and check concept drift with a train-on-year-i / test-on-year-j accuracy matrix.
84	
85	**Sampling.** Every year is subsampled to the same size `n = min(rows per year)` (3,000 with the current data; computed, not hard-coded), using `random_state=42`, stratified so each sample has equal malware and benign counts. Both classes are pooled per year, so drift here includes any change in the malware/goodware mix inside a year; the balanced sampling removes that source.
86	
87	**Functions.**
88	- `subsample_years(df, n: int | None = None, seed: int = SEED) -> dict[int, pd.DataFrame]`: equal-size, class-balanced sample per year; `n=None` uses the smallest year.
89	- `ks_feature_table(a: pd.DataFrame, b: pd.DataFrame, features: list[str]) -> pd.DataFrame`: runs `scipy.stats.ks_2samp` on each feature; returns columns `feature, ks_stat, p_value, skipped`. A feature constant in both samples (same single value) is marked `skipped` (NaN stat/p) and counted, not tested.
90	- `ks_all_pairs(samples, features)` runs KS once for all 28 year pairs; `ks_year_pairs(pairs, mode)` summarises them. `mode="all"` (every pair, shown as a year x year matrix), `mode="vs_2014"` (each year 2015-2021 vs 2014) or `mode="consecutive"` (year vs previous year). Returns one row per pair: `year_a, year_b, n_tested, n_skipped, mean_ks, share_significant`.
91	- `bonferroni_significant(p_values: np.ndarray, alpha: float = 0.05) -> np.ndarray`: boolean mask with `p < alpha / m`, `m` = number of tested (non-skipped) features.
92	- `top_drifting_features(samples, features, k: int = 20) -> pd.DataFrame`: top-k features by mean KS statistic across the "vs 2014" comparisons (also lists the per-year KS for each).
93	- `most_different_years(pair_table: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame`: pairs ranked by mean KS.
94	- `concept_drift_matrix(samples: dict[int, pd.DataFrame], features, seed: int = SEED) -> pd.DataFrame`: for each year i, fit log1p + StandardScaler + `LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, random_state=42)` on year i's sample only (scaler fit on that year only), compute accuracy on every year j's sample (i==j uses a held-out 30% split of that year, so the diagonal is not training accuracy). Returns an 8x8 accuracy DataFrame.
95	- `run_drift_analysis(df) -> dict[str, pd.DataFrame]`: runs the above and writes `results/step2_ks_vs_2014.csv`, `step2_ks_consecutive.csv`, `step2_top20_features.csv`, `step2_accuracy_matrix.csv` and optional PNG heatmaps.
96	
97	**Runtime.** 7 + 7 year pairs x ~1,800 `ks_2samp` calls on 3,000 points is well under a minute.
98	
99	**Caveat to state in the report.** With 3,000 samples per year the KS test is very sensitive, so most features may be "significant" after Bonferroni; the mean KS statistic (effect size) is the more useful number. Features all-zero in both samples are skipped and reported as a count. Duplicate rows (many in 2014-2018) and heavily tied count data mean the samples are not independent, so KS p-values and "share significant" are inflated; the KS statistic (effect size) is the main signal. The subsampling is unchanged.
100	
101	**Report.** `docs/step2_drift_analysis.md`: method, sample size, skipped counts, table of mean KS and share significant per pair, top-20 drifting features (Dalvik signatures), which years differ most, the accuracy matrix and what it says about concept drift.
102	
103	**Testing.** Synthetic: identical samples give KS 0 and none significant; a shifted feature gives a high KS and is flagged; constant-in-both features are skipped and counted; `bonferroni_significant` uses `alpha / m` with `m` excluding skipped features (hand-computed case); `subsample_years` gives equal sizes, is reproducible with seed 42 and is class balanced; matrix is square and indexed by years; top-k returns k rows sorted descending. Real data (skipped if absent): the result tables have 7 rows each.
104	
105	---
106	
107	## Step 3: Preprocess (`src/preprocess.py`)
108	
109	**Approach.** `log1p` to tame the heavy tail (counts up to ~92,000), drop features that are non-zero in fewer than `MIN_SUPPORT = 10` training rows (this includes all-zero columns), then `StandardScaler` fit on training years only, then clip the scaled values to a fixed ±`Z_CLIP = 10` (a constant, identical for train and test, nothing learned from any data). Output float32. The minimum-support filter removes the worst near-constant columns, but it does not stop extreme z-scores on drifted test years (measured: max abs z 212.7 in 2018, 150.6 in training), so the clip is what bounds them. **Changed after review comment 1** (the filter alone does not meet its stated purpose).
110	
111	**Functions.**
112	- `check_no_overlap(train_years: Iterable[int], test_years: Iterable[int]) -> None`: raises `ValueError` if they share a year, if either is empty, or if `max(train_years) >= min(test_years)`. Not called by Step 2's `concept_drift_matrix` (exempt, see section 0).
113	- `split_by_year(df, train_years, test_years) -> tuple[pd.DataFrame, pd.DataFrame]`: calls `check_no_overlap`, returns the train and test frames (rows selected by `year`).
114	- `apply_log1p(X: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray`: `np.log1p` as float32; raises on negative input.
115	- `nonzero_feature_mask(X_train: np.ndarray, min_support: int = MIN_SUPPORT) -> np.ndarray`: boolean mask of columns with at least `min_support` (10) non-zero values in the training rows only. `MIN_SUPPORT = 10` is added to `src/config.py`.
116	- `class Preprocessor` (sklearn-like fit/transform, not a `BaseEstimator`): `fit(X_train_raw: np.ndarray) -> Preprocessor` (applies log1p, learns the mask, fits `StandardScaler`), `transform(X_raw: np.ndarray, clip: bool = True) -> np.ndarray` (log1p, mask, scale, clip to ±`Z_CLIP`; `clip=False` only for reporting), `fit_transform`, attribute `kept_features_` (names/indices). Raises if `transform` is called before `fit`.
117	- `prepare_split(df, train_years, test_years) -> dict`: returns `X_train, y_train, years_train, X_test, y_test, years_test, preprocessor`; the preprocessor is fit on the training rows only.
118	- `make_tuning_split(df) -> dict`: same, with train 2014-2015 and validate 2016.
119	
120	**Decision flagged.** Dropping all-zero training columns is only a size reduction (such columns have zero variance and no information in training). Dropping columns with 1-9 non-zero training rows is a deliberate extra filter (support below 10), chosen because a tiny training std turns ordinary test values into z-scores in the hundreds. A column that is non-zero only in a later year is lost for the static model. That loss is real drift and is reported (count of columns active in test years but dropped). Step 7 refits the mask on each window, which recovers them.
121	
122	**Report.** `docs/step3_preprocessing.md`: log1p and why, number of columns dropped (split into all-zero and low-support 1-9 rows), the minimum-support rule (`MIN_SUPPORT = 10`, training rows only) and why, scaler details, the split table above, and the five leakage rules.
123	
124	**Testing.** Synthetic: scaler mean/std come from training rows only (train mean ~0, std ~1; test is not centred on its own mean); the mask comes from training only (a column non-zero only in a test row is dropped); near-constant column: a column non-zero in 9 training rows is dropped and one non-zero in 10 is kept, and a test value in a dropped column cannot produce a large z-score; `log1p` equals `np.log1p`, negative input raises; `check_no_overlap` raises on overlap and on train years after test years (e.g. train 2018-2020 / test 2014); `transform` before `fit` raises. Leakage test on the real or synthetic frame: no `year` appears in both the train and test outputs of `prepare_split`, and training years are exactly 2014-2016. Changing test rows must not change the fitted scaler (fit twice, compare `mean_`).
125	
126	---
127	
128	## Step 4: Classifiers (`src/models.py`)
129	
130	**Approach.** Three scikit-learn models, all `random_state=42`, trained on the preprocessed 2014-2016 data.
131	
132	**Functions.**
133	- `build_model(name: str) -> sklearn estimator`: `name` in `{"logreg", "random_forest", "sgd"}`; raises `ValueError` otherwise.
134	- `train_model(name: str, X_train: np.ndarray, y_train: np.ndarray) -> estimator`: builds and fits.
135	- `train_all(X_train, y_train) -> dict[str, estimator]`.
136	- `train_all_from_split(split: dict) -> dict[str, estimator]`: the static Step 4 entry point; wraps `train_all` and raises if `set(split["years_train"]) <= set(TRAIN_YEARS)` is false. This guard is for the static 2014-2016 model only; Step 7 windows (2017+) do not use it. Step 7 uses `window_years` plus `check_no_overlap` instead (see Step 7).
137	- `tune_logreg(tune_split: dict) -> dict`: only if time allows: small grid on `C` using train 2014-2015 / validate 2016, scoring F1 (malware); returns best params and the grid scores.
138	- `MODEL_NAMES: tuple[str, ...]`.
139	
140	**Models and hyperparameter justification.**
141	- `LogisticRegression(class_weight="balanced", max_iter=1000, solver="lbfgs", C=1.0, random_state=42)`: linear baseline that works well on scaled sparse-ish counts; `balanced` protects against label imbalance if present (the data is balanced per year, but later use may not be); `max_iter=1000` so lbfgs converges on ~1,000 standardized features (a `ConvergenceWarning` is treated as a problem to report); `C=1.0` is the default, changed only if tuning on 2016 says so.
142	- `RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, n_jobs=-1, random_state=42)`: non-linear model that is insensitive to feature scale; 200 trees is a point where accuracy usually plateaus while training stays within a minute or two on ~54,000 rows; other settings default (unbounded depth, `max_features="sqrt"`).
143	- `SGDClassifier(loss="log_loss", penalty="l2", alpha=1e-4, max_iter=1000, tol=1e-3, random_state=42)`: a logistic model trained by SGD, needed because Step 7 uses `partial_fit` (LogisticRegression and RandomForest have none). No `class_weight`: sklearn rejects `class_weight="balanced"` in `partial_fit`, and the data is balanced per year. `alpha=1e-4` is the sklearn default and a standard regularisation level for ~50k samples. For `partial_fit` the first call passes `classes=[0, 1]`.
144	
145	**Report.** `docs/step4_models.md`: the three models, why each, the hyperparameter table and justification, training time per model, any convergence warnings, and tuning results if run.
146	
147	**Testing.** Synthetic separable data: each model trains and predicts both classes with accuracy above chance (e.g. > 0.9); `build_model` returns the right class with `random_state == 42` (and `class_weight == "balanced"` for logreg only, `n_estimators == 200` where applicable); unknown name raises; the model returned by `build_model("sgd")` can be fit and then called with `partial_fit(X, y)` without error (not just "has the method"); same seed gives identical predictions twice; training with rows from a test year raises (guard checked via `years_train` argument in `train_all_from_split`, see below). A test that the training matrix has only years 2014-2016, and that `train_all_from_split` raises on a split containing a test year.
148	
149	---
150	
151	## Steps 5 and 6: Evaluation (`src/evaluate.py`)
152	
153	**Approach.** Predict on held-out test years 2017-2021 only. Malware (1) is the positive class. Step 5 is the pooled table; Step 6 is the per-year breakdown.
154	
155	**Functions.**
156	- `compute_metrics(y_true: np.ndarray, y_pred: np.ndarray) -> dict[str, float]`: `accuracy, precision, recall, f1`, using `pos_label=1`, `zero_division=0`.
157	- `evaluate_model(model, X_test, y_test) -> dict[str, float]`.
158	- `pooled_table(models: dict, X_test, y_test) -> pd.DataFrame`: one row per classifier, columns `model, accuracy, precision, recall, f1, n_test` (Step 5; pooled over 2017-2021).
159	- `per_year_table(models: dict, X_test, y_test, years_test) -> pd.DataFrame`: one row per (model, year), same metrics plus `year, n`; only years in `TEST_YEARS` (Step 6).
160	- `drift_summary(per_year: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame`: per model: first-test-year F1, last-test-year F1, drop, and the F1 slope across years.
161	- `assert_test_years_only(years: np.ndarray) -> None`: raises if any year is outside `TEST_YEARS`.
162	- `sensitivity_tables(models: dict, X_test, y_test, years_test, dup_mask: np.ndarray) -> tuple[pd.DataFrame, pd.DataFrame]`: the same pooled and per-year tables restricted to test rows where `dup_mask` is False (no exact duplicate in 2014-2016), with a `n_excluded` column; `dup_mask` comes from `train_duplicate_mask` (Step 1). Saved as `results/step5_pooled_no_dup.*` and `results/step6_per_year_no_dup.*`.
163	- `save_table(df: pd.DataFrame, stem: str) -> None`: writes `results/<stem>.csv` and `results/<stem>.md` (Markdown table with fixed rounding to 4 decimals).
164	- Entry point for Steps 5 (and later 6): `main.run_step5(df=None, split=None, models=None) -> dict[str, pd.DataFrame]`, consistent with `run_step1` to `run_step4` (the earlier `run_evaluation(df)` was not built). It reuses the Step 4 models when given, otherwise trains them on 2014-2016; writes `results/step5_metrics.*` (with a `baseline_accuracy` column), `results/step5_confusion.*` and `results/step5_pooled_no_dup.*`. Step 6 is `main.run_step6(df=None, split=None, models=None)` (same pattern; reuses the Step 4 models, never refits on a test year). It writes `results/step6_by_year.*` (columns `classifier, year, n, accuracy, precision, recall, f1`; `by_year_export` renames `model` to `classifier`), `results/step6_baseline_by_year.*` (`year_baseline_table`: n, class counts, majority-class accuracy per year), `results/step6_drift_summary.*` (`drift_summary`), `results/step6_per_year_no_dup.*` and the figure `results/step6_by_year.png` (`plot_by_year`; F1 and accuracy by year; replaces the planned name `step6_f1_by_year.png` as the lead engineer asked).
165	
166	**Notes.** Pooled metrics weight years by size (2017-2018 are 6x larger than 2019-2021), so the per-year table is the primary view; the report says so.
167	
168	**Reports.** `docs/step5_evaluation.md` (pooled table, accuracy as the primary metric, plus precision/recall/F1 and a short comparison). `docs/step6_test_results.md` (per-year table for each classifier, how performance changes as data drifts, link to Step 2 findings).
169	
170	**Testing.** Hand-computed confusion matrix (e.g. TP=3, FP=1, FN=2, TN=4) gives the exact accuracy, precision, recall and F1; metrics treat 1 as positive (swapping labels changes precision/recall); all-benign predictions give recall 0 and precision 0 without raising; `per_year_table` has one row per model per test year, the row counts `n` sum to the pooled `n_test`, and weighted per-year accuracy equals the pooled accuracy; `assert_test_years_only` raises on a training year; files are written with the expected columns. `train_duplicate_mask` flags a hand-built test row identical to a training row and not a unique one; `sensitivity_tables` excludes exactly the flagged rows and `n + n_excluded` equals the full test count.
171	
172	---
173	
174	## Step 7: Sustainable approach (`src/sustainable.py`)
175	
176	**Approach.** Compare four strategies on the same test years (2017-2021), same metrics (accuracy, precision, recall, F1; malware positive), reported per year and pooled. Rule for all of them: year t is predicted before any of its rows is used for training or for fitting preprocessing.
177	
178	| Strategy | Training data used to predict year t |
179	|---|---|
180	| (a) static | 2014-2016 only, never updated (this is the Step 4/6 model) |
181	| (b) expanding window | all years before t (2014..t-1); preprocessing and model refit from scratch for each t |
182	| (c) sliding window | the 3 years before t (t-3..t-1); preprocessing and model refit for each t |
183	| (d) incremental | SGD fit on 2014-2016, then for t = 2017..2021: predict t, then `partial_fit` on t (test-then-train) |
184	
185	For t=2017 the windows in (b) and (c) are both 2014-2016, so (a)-(c) agree on 2017; they differ from 2018 on.
186	
187	**Functions.**
188	- Step 7 guard: every Step 7 fit goes through `window_years` (which raises if any returned year is >= t) and then `check_no_overlap(window, [t])`. `train_all_from_split` is not used here.
189	- `window_years(strategy: str, t: int) -> tuple[int, ...]`: training years for strategy `"static"`, `"expanding"` or `"sliding"` at test year t (static: 2014-2016; expanding: 2014..t-1; sliding: t-3..t-1); raises if t is not in `TEST_YEARS` or if any returned year is >= t.
190	- `run_window_strategy(df, strategy: str, model_name: str = "logreg") -> pd.DataFrame`: for each t: `check_no_overlap(window, [t])`, fit a new `Preprocessor` and model on the window only, predict t, compute metrics; returns one row per test year.
191	- `run_incremental(df, model_name: str = "sgd") -> pd.DataFrame`: initial `fit` of `Preprocessor` and SGD on 2014-2016 (preprocessor frozen afterwards, so later years use the same mask and scaler: a limitation noted in the report); loop over t, record the prediction on t first, then `partial_fit` on year t with the true labels. Returns one row per test year.
192	- `run_all_strategies(df, split=None, models=None, step4_seconds=None, rf=True) -> pd.DataFrame`: concatenates (a)-(d) with `strategy` and `classifier` columns, one row per (strategy, classifier, test year); static rows come from the Step 4 models when given. **Changed in Step 7:** the pooled rows are not in this table (a `year` column stays numeric); `pooled_by_strategy` writes them separately.
193	- `compare_to_static(results: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame`: per strategy and year, difference in F1 and accuracy against the static model.
194	- `run_sustainable(df, split=None, models=None, step4_seconds=None, rf=True) -> dict[str, pd.DataFrame]`: writes `results/step7_strategies.*` (columns `strategy, classifier, year, n, accuracy, precision, recall, f1`; replaces the planned name `step7_strategy_metrics`, as the lead engineer asked), `step7_strategies_detail.*` (adds confusion counts, training seconds, rows and window), `step7_pooled.*`, `step7_vs_static.*`, `step7_summary.*` (mean F1, worst year), `step7_cost.*`, `step7_window_composition.*` and `step7_f1_by_year.png` (F1 and accuracy by year, dashed always-malware F1 0.667 and chance accuracy 0.5).
195	- Helpers: `year_arrays`, `fit_on_years` (the single place every window fit goes through: `check_no_overlap` plus a `max(years) < t` assertion), `static_from_models`, `pooled_by_strategy`, `summary_table`, `cost_table`, `window_composition`, `plot_strategies`. `run_incremental` also asserts before every prediction that no year seen so far is >= t.
196	
197	**Model choice and decision flagged.** Windows (b)-(c) and the static baseline use LogisticRegression so that all five refits finish in a few minutes; (d) uses SGD. A fair isolation of "incremental vs retrain" would also run SGD under (a)-(c); I will add SGD-static as an extra row (cheap) so the incremental gain is compared with the same model family. RandomForest is run for (a) and (b) only (not (c) or (d)); measured, it fit within the budget. Runtime estimate: ~54,000-90,000 rows x ~1,000 features per LR refit, 5 refits per strategy; to be measured, not assumed.
198	
199	**Assumption to state.** Labels for year t become available only after year t ends (test-then-train); a real labeling delay would hurt (d), (b) and (c) in practice. The report states this. Not simulated here.
200	
201	**Row-count imbalance (to state in the report).** Years 2014-2018 have 18,000 rows each and 2019-2021 have 3,000, so the expanding window is dominated by old data and the 3-year window for 2021 (2018-2020) is 18,000 of 24,000 rows from 2018. The report notes that "retraining helps or not" may partly reflect this row-count imbalance rather than recency alone, and lists each window's year composition (rows per year in the training window for every strategy and test year; also saved as `results/step7_window_composition.csv`). No equal-rows variant is run.
202	
203	**Report.** `docs/step7_sustainable_approach.md`: the four strategies, the table of F1/accuracy per year, the window composition table and the imbalance note above, comparison with the static model, cost (training time per strategy), conclusions that feed the one-page report.
204	
205	**Testing.** Synthetic multi-year frame with an injected drift (class boundary shifts each year): `window_years` returns exactly the specified years (including edge cases t=2017 and t=2021); for every strategy and every t, `max(window) < t` (the no-test-year-in-training check, run through a spy that records the years passed to `fit`); `run_incremental` records predictions on t before `partial_fit` on t (verified with a stub model that logs call order and, separately, by checking the year-t labels are not seen at prediction time); static results are identical to the Step 6 model's results; result tables have one row per test year per strategy and the expected columns; on the injected-drift data the retraining/incremental strategies do not do worse than the static one in the final year (sanity check, not a performance claim).
206	
207	---
208	
209	## Cross-cutting test plan (tester)
210	- `tests/test_stepN_*.py` per step with synthetic data in `tmp_path`; real-data tests marked and skipped when `input_data/` is absent.
211	- A project-wide leakage test: every call that fits anything records the years it saw (via a spy/wrapper); none of 2017-2021 may appear before its own prediction. Applies to Steps 3-7; `drift.py` (Step 2) is exempt.
212	- `python harness.py test N` for one step and `python harness.py test all` for all.
213	
214	## Implementation order and commits
215	One commit per task (about 300 added lines max): config + data, then drift, then preprocess, then models, then evaluate, then sustainable, then main and docs. Each step is followed by a review and test cycle outside this plan.
216	
217	## Points where I disagree or want a decision
218	1. The accuracy matrix in Step 2 trains on later years and predicts earlier ones; this is a diagnostic only, not used for any design choice, and is exempt from the leakage rules (section 0).
219	2. Step 7 (d) freezes the scaler and zero-column mask from 2014-2016; an alternative (updating the scaler with `partial_fit`) is possible but not planned.
220	3. Cross-year duplicates (item 5 above) stay in the main results; the sensitivity row reports the effect.
221

# PLAN.md: Project 2 plan (Steps 1-7)

Author: builder agent. Status: initial version (Step 0), before review.
Data facts used here come from AGENTS.md. Nothing in this plan has been run yet; no result is claimed.

## 0. Global decisions

### Train/test split by year

| Role | Years | Use |
|---|---|---|
| Train | 2014, 2015, 2016 | fit preprocessing and models |
| Tuning (only if needed) | train on 2014-2015, validate on 2016 | choose hyperparameters; then refit on 2014-2016 |
| Test | 2017, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021 | evaluation only; every metric is reported pooled AND per year |

### How leakage between years is prevented

1. One function `check_no_overlap(train_years, test_years)` (in `src/preprocess.py`) raises `ValueError` if either set is empty, if the sets intersect, or if `max(train_years) >= min(test_years)` (training years must all precede test years). Every train/predict call in Steps 3-7 goes through it.
   - **Exemption (Step 2).** `concept_drift_matrix` in `src/drift.py` is diagnostic: it fits a scaler and a model on each single year (including 2017-2021) and predicts other years, so it does not obey the train-2014-2016 rule or `check_no_overlap`. Nothing it produces feeds Steps 3-7 (no features, hyperparameters or split choices). The leakage tests skip `drift.py`; they apply to Steps 3-7 only.
2. Every fitted object (zero-column mask, `StandardScaler`, classifiers) is fit on the training rows only. Test rows are only passed to `transform` / `predict`. `log1p` is stateless, so it cannot leak.
3. Tuning never touches 2017-2021.
4. Step 7: year t is predicted before it is used for training (see Step 7). Expanding/sliding windows refit preprocessing on the window only.
5. Cross-year duplicates: the 2014-2018 files have many duplicate rows and repeated apknames. Step 1 reports (a) exact duplicate feature rows within a year and (b) apknames or identical feature vectors shared between a training year and a test year. I keep all rows by default (AGENTS.md); no rows are removed from the main results. Step 1 reports, per test year, the count and share of test rows whose exact feature vector also occurs in the training years (2014-2016). Steps 5 and 6 add a sensitivity row (`subset = "no_train_duplicate"`) with metrics on only the test rows that have no exact duplicate in the training years, and state in the report how many test rows were excluded.
6. Step 2 (KS tests, accuracy matrix) is descriptive. Its output is never used to select features, hyperparameters or the split.

### Conventions (from AGENTS.md)
random_state=42; features as float32/int32; pathlib paths relative to the repo root; docstrings and type hints on every function; one module per concern; cache in the git-ignored `cache/` folder (see `load_all` in Step 1 for the cache rules); small commits tagged `[builder]`.

### Shared constants (`src/config.py`)
`ROOT`, `DATA_DIR`, `RESULTS_DIR`, `DOCS_DIR`, `SEED = 42`, `MIN_SUPPORT = 10`, `CACHE_DIR`, `CACHE_SCHEMA_VERSION`, `TRAIN_YEARS = (2014, 2015, 2016)`, `TEST_YEARS = (2017, ..., 2021)`, `TUNE_TRAIN_YEARS = (2014, 2015)`, `TUNE_VAL_YEAR = 2016`, `N_RAW_COLUMNS = 1849`, `LABEL_COL = "label"`, `YEAR_COL = "year"`.

### Entry point (`src/main.py`)
`main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> int`. `python -m src.main` runs Steps 1-7 in order; `--step N` (1-7) runs one step (running it first runs any earlier step it needs, using the cache). Prints a short summary, writes `results/`. Target: under about 15 minutes in total (see runtime notes per step).

---

## Changes after review

Source: `reviews/step0_plan_review.md` (Decision log). Comment 10 was Rejected and is not applied.

| Comment | Change in PLAN.md |
|---|---|
| 1 | SGD no longer uses `class_weight` (rejected by `partial_fit`); test must call `partial_fit` on `build_model("sgd")`. |
| 2 | Section 0: explicit exemption; `concept_drift_matrix` fits on single years, leakage tests skip `drift.py`. |
| 3 | `MIN_SUPPORT = 10`: keep columns non-zero in at least 10 training rows; documented in step 3 report; near-constant column test. |
| 4 | Step 1 reports test rows duplicated in 2014-2016 (`train_duplicate_mask`); Steps 5 and 6 add a no-duplicate sensitivity row; main results keep all rows. |
| 5 | `check_no_overlap` also requires `max(train_years) < min(test_years)`; Step 2 matrix exempt. |
| 6 | Cache keyed on file names, sizes, mtimes and schema version; column names stored; schema checks rerun on load; stored in git-ignored `cache/`. |
| 7 | `train_all_from_split` moved into the Step 4 function list; Step 7 guard is `window_years` plus `check_no_overlap`. |
| 8 | Step 7 report notes the row-count imbalance and lists each window's year composition. No equal-rows variant. |
| 9 | Step 2 report caveat: duplicates and ties inflate KS p-values; effect size is the main signal. |
| 11 | `list_data_files` runs `parse_filename` on every CSV so stray files raise; stray-file test added. |

---

## Step 1: Prepare the data (`src/data.py`)

**Approach.** Read the 16 CSVs, take year and class only from the file name, drop `apkname`, add `label` (malware=1, benign=0) and `year`, validate the schema, and combine.

**Functions.**
- `parse_filename(name: str) -> tuple[int, int]`: regex `^sampled_(\d{4})_(malware|benign)_api\.csv$` on the base name; returns `(year, label)`. Raises `ValueError` on any other name, a year outside 2014-2021, or a bad class.
- `list_data_files(data_dir: Path = DATA_DIR) -> list[Path]`: lists every `*.csv` in `data_dir` and runs `parse_filename` on each, so a stray or misnamed CSV raises `ValueError` (not ignored). Returns the sorted list; also raises if there is not exactly one malware and one benign file for each of 2014-2021 (16 files).
- `load_file(path: Path) -> pd.DataFrame`: reads the CSV, checks the shape is `(n, 1849)` and the first column is `apkname`, drops it, casts the 1,848 features to int32, appends `label` (int8) and `year` (int16) from `parse_filename`. Raises `ValueError` if the column count is not 1,849 or any value is negative or missing. Does not assert a row count.
- `read_apknames(path: Path) -> pd.Series`: the `apkname` column only (for the duplicate/overlap audit; never used as a feature).
- `load_year(year: int, data_dir: Path = DATA_DIR) -> pd.DataFrame`: concatenates that year's malware and benign files.
- `validate_feature_order(frames: list[pd.DataFrame]) -> None`: raises if any frame's feature columns differ from the first one in names or order.
- `combine_years(frames: dict[int, pd.DataFrame]) -> pd.DataFrame`: concatenates years in order (calls `validate_feature_order`); `ignore_index=True`.
- `load_all(data_dir: Path = DATA_DIR, use_cache: bool = True) -> pd.DataFrame`: the whole dataset (~100,000 x 1,850 incl. label, year). Cache rules: stored in `cache/` (git-ignored; `CACHE_DIR` in `src/config.py`). The cache key is a hash of each CSV's file name, size and mtime plus `CACHE_SCHEMA_VERSION` (a constant bumped whenever `src/data.py` changes how data is built). The cache file holds the feature column names with the arrays; on every cache load the schema checks run again (1,848 feature columns in the stored order, `label`/`year` present, no negatives). A key mismatch or failed check rebuilds from the CSVs. If this proves complicated, the cache is dropped rather than weakened.
- `cache_key(data_dir: Path) -> str`: the hash described above (used by `load_all`).
- `feature_columns(df: pd.DataFrame) -> list[str]`: all columns except `label` and `year` (1,848 names).
- `summarize_data(df: pd.DataFrame, data_dir: Path = DATA_DIR) -> pd.DataFrame`: one row per year: files loaded, rows, feature columns, malware count, benign count, exact duplicate rows, all-zero feature columns, apknames repeated within the year, and the number of rows in the year whose feature vector also occurs in an earlier year, and (test years) the number and share of rows whose feature vector occurs in 2014-2016.
- `train_duplicate_mask(df: pd.DataFrame, train_years=TRAIN_YEARS) -> np.ndarray`: boolean mask over all rows of `df`, True where the row's exact feature vector also occurs in a training-year row (for training-year rows themselves it is not used). Used by Steps 1, 5 and 6.
- `write_data_summary(summary: pd.DataFrame, path: Path) -> None`: Markdown + CSV.

**Report.** `docs/step1_data_summary.md`: files per year, real row counts (not 1,500), 1,849 raw columns and 1,848 features after dropping `apkname`, malware/benign counts per year, duplicate/overlap audit, dtype and memory use. Table also saved to `results/step1_data_summary.csv`.

**Testing.** Synthetic CSVs in `tmp_path`: `parse_filename` accepts valid names and rejects bad ones (wrong year, wrong class, extra suffix, path with directories); `load_file` drops the first column, gives 1,848 features, correct label from name, wrong column count raises; mismatched feature order raises; `combine_years` row count equals the sum of inputs; label and year columns are right. `list_data_files` raises on a stray CSV (e.g. `notes.csv`) in the folder and on a missing or duplicated year/class file. Cache: `cache_key` changes when a file's size or mtime changes or the schema version changes; a second `load_all` returns an equal frame; touching a CSV forces a rebuild; a cache with altered column names or order is rejected. Integration test (skipped if `input_data/` is absent): 16 files, 1,849 raw columns each, 18,000 rows per year for 2014-2018 and 3,000 for 2019-2021, equal malware and benign counts, no NaN.

---

## Step 2: Handle data drift (`src/drift.py`)

**Approach.** Measure feature drift with the two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, and check concept drift with a train-on-year-i / test-on-year-j accuracy matrix.

**Sampling.** Every year is subsampled to the same size `n = min(rows per year)` (3,000 with the current data; computed, not hard-coded), using `random_state=42`, stratified so each sample has equal malware and benign counts. Both classes are pooled per year, so drift here includes any change in the malware/goodware mix inside a year; the balanced sampling removes that source.

**Functions.**
- `subsample_years(df, n: int | None = None, seed: int = SEED) -> dict[int, pd.DataFrame]`: equal-size, class-balanced sample per year; `n=None` uses the smallest year.
- `ks_feature_table(a: pd.DataFrame, b: pd.DataFrame, features: list[str]) -> pd.DataFrame`: runs `scipy.stats.ks_2samp` on each feature; returns columns `feature, ks_stat, p_value, skipped`. A feature constant in both samples (same single value) is marked `skipped` (NaN stat/p) and counted, not tested.
- `ks_all_pairs(samples, features)` runs KS once for all 28 year pairs; `ks_year_pairs(pairs, mode)` summarises them. `mode="all"` (every pair, shown as a year x year matrix), `mode="vs_2014"` (each year 2015-2021 vs 2014) or `mode="consecutive"` (year vs previous year). Returns one row per pair: `year_a, year_b, n_tested, n_skipped, mean_ks, share_significant`.
- `bonferroni_significant(p_values: np.ndarray, alpha: float = 0.05) -> np.ndarray`: boolean mask with `p < alpha / m`, `m` = number of tested (non-skipped) features.
- `top_drifting_features(samples, features, k: int = 20) -> pd.DataFrame`: top-k features by mean KS statistic across the "vs 2014" comparisons (also lists the per-year KS for each).
- `most_different_years(pair_table: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame`: pairs ranked by mean KS.
- `concept_drift_matrix(samples: dict[int, pd.DataFrame], features, seed: int = SEED) -> pd.DataFrame`: for each year i, fit log1p + StandardScaler + `LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, random_state=42)` on year i's sample only (scaler fit on that year only), compute accuracy on every year j's sample (i==j uses a held-out 30% split of that year, so the diagonal is not training accuracy). Returns an 8x8 accuracy DataFrame.
- `run_drift_analysis(df) -> dict[str, pd.DataFrame]`: runs the above and writes `results/step2_ks_vs_2014.csv`, `step2_ks_consecutive.csv`, `step2_top20_features.csv`, `step2_accuracy_matrix.csv` and optional PNG heatmaps.

**Runtime.** 7 + 7 year pairs x ~1,800 `ks_2samp` calls on 3,000 points is well under a minute.

**Caveat to state in the report.** With 3,000 samples per year the KS test is very sensitive, so most features may be "significant" after Bonferroni; the mean KS statistic (effect size) is the more useful number. Features all-zero in both samples are skipped and reported as a count. Duplicate rows (many in 2014-2018) and heavily tied count data mean the samples are not independent, so KS p-values and "share significant" are inflated; the KS statistic (effect size) is the main signal. The subsampling is unchanged.

**Report.** `docs/step2_drift_analysis.md`: method, sample size, skipped counts, table of mean KS and share significant per pair, top-20 drifting features (Dalvik signatures), which years differ most, the accuracy matrix and what it says about concept drift.

**Testing.** Synthetic: identical samples give KS 0 and none significant; a shifted feature gives a high KS and is flagged; constant-in-both features are skipped and counted; `bonferroni_significant` uses `alpha / m` with `m` excluding skipped features (hand-computed case); `subsample_years` gives equal sizes, is reproducible with seed 42 and is class balanced; matrix is square and indexed by years; top-k returns k rows sorted descending. Real data (skipped if absent): the result tables have 7 rows each.

---

## Step 3: Preprocess (`src/preprocess.py`)

**Approach.** `log1p` to tame the heavy tail (counts up to ~92,000), drop features that are non-zero in fewer than `MIN_SUPPORT = 10` training rows (this includes all-zero columns), then `StandardScaler` fit on training years only, then clip the scaled values to a fixed ±`Z_CLIP = 10` (a constant, identical for train and test, nothing learned from any data). Output float32. The minimum-support filter removes the worst near-constant columns, but it does not stop extreme z-scores on drifted test years (measured: max abs z 212.7 in 2018, 150.6 in training), so the clip is what bounds them. **Changed after review comment 1** (the filter alone does not meet its stated purpose).

**Functions.**
- `check_no_overlap(train_years: Iterable[int], test_years: Iterable[int]) -> None`: raises `ValueError` if they share a year, if either is empty, or if `max(train_years) >= min(test_years)`. Not called by Step 2's `concept_drift_matrix` (exempt, see section 0).
- `split_by_year(df, train_years, test_years) -> tuple[pd.DataFrame, pd.DataFrame]`: calls `check_no_overlap`, returns the train and test frames (rows selected by `year`).
- `apply_log1p(X: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray`: `np.log1p` as float32; raises on negative input.
- `nonzero_feature_mask(X_train: np.ndarray, min_support: int = MIN_SUPPORT) -> np.ndarray`: boolean mask of columns with at least `min_support` (10) non-zero values in the training rows only. `MIN_SUPPORT = 10` is added to `src/config.py`.
- `class Preprocessor` (sklearn-like fit/transform, not a `BaseEstimator`): `fit(X_train_raw: np.ndarray) -> Preprocessor` (applies log1p, learns the mask, fits `StandardScaler`), `transform(X_raw: np.ndarray, clip: bool = True) -> np.ndarray` (log1p, mask, scale, clip to ±`Z_CLIP`; `clip=False` only for reporting), `fit_transform`, attribute `kept_features_` (names/indices). Raises if `transform` is called before `fit`.
- `prepare_split(df, train_years, test_years) -> dict`: returns `X_train, y_train, years_train, X_test, y_test, years_test, preprocessor`; the preprocessor is fit on the training rows only.
- `make_tuning_split(df) -> dict`: same, with train 2014-2015 and validate 2016.

**Decision flagged.** Dropping all-zero training columns is only a size reduction (such columns have zero variance and no information in training). Dropping columns with 1-9 non-zero training rows is a deliberate extra filter (support below 10), chosen because a tiny training std turns ordinary test values into z-scores in the hundreds. A column that is non-zero only in a later year is lost for the static model. That loss is real drift and is reported (count of columns active in test years but dropped). Step 7 refits the mask on each window, which recovers them.

**Report.** `docs/step3_preprocessing.md`: log1p and why, number of columns dropped (split into all-zero and low-support 1-9 rows), the minimum-support rule (`MIN_SUPPORT = 10`, training rows only) and why, scaler details, the split table above, and the five leakage rules.

**Testing.** Synthetic: scaler mean/std come from training rows only (train mean ~0, std ~1; test is not centred on its own mean); the mask comes from training only (a column non-zero only in a test row is dropped); near-constant column: a column non-zero in 9 training rows is dropped and one non-zero in 10 is kept, and a test value in a dropped column cannot produce a large z-score; `log1p` equals `np.log1p`, negative input raises; `check_no_overlap` raises on overlap and on train years after test years (e.g. train 2018-2020 / test 2014); `transform` before `fit` raises. Leakage test on the real or synthetic frame: no `year` appears in both the train and test outputs of `prepare_split`, and training years are exactly 2014-2016. Changing test rows must not change the fitted scaler (fit twice, compare `mean_`).

---

## Step 4: Classifiers (`src/models.py`)

**Approach.** Three scikit-learn models, all `random_state=42`, trained on the preprocessed 2014-2016 data.

**Functions.**
- `build_model(name: str) -> sklearn estimator`: `name` in `{"logreg", "random_forest", "sgd"}`; raises `ValueError` otherwise.
- `train_model(name: str, X_train: np.ndarray, y_train: np.ndarray) -> estimator`: builds and fits.
- `train_all(X_train, y_train) -> dict[str, estimator]`.
- `train_all_from_split(split: dict) -> dict[str, estimator]`: the static Step 4 entry point; wraps `train_all` and raises if `set(split["years_train"]) <= set(TRAIN_YEARS)` is false. This guard is for the static 2014-2016 model only; Step 7 windows (2017+) do not use it. Step 7 uses `window_years` plus `check_no_overlap` instead (see Step 7).
- `tune_logreg(tune_split: dict) -> dict`: only if time allows: small grid on `C` using train 2014-2015 / validate 2016, scoring F1 (malware); returns best params and the grid scores.
- `MODEL_NAMES: tuple[str, ...]`.

**Models and hyperparameter justification.**
- `LogisticRegression(class_weight="balanced", max_iter=1000, solver="lbfgs", C=1.0, random_state=42)`: linear baseline that works well on scaled sparse-ish counts; `balanced` protects against label imbalance if present (the data is balanced per year, but later use may not be); `max_iter=1000` so lbfgs converges on ~1,000 standardized features (a `ConvergenceWarning` is treated as a problem to report); `C=1.0` is the default, changed only if tuning on 2016 says so.
- `RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, n_jobs=-1, random_state=42)`: non-linear model that is insensitive to feature scale; 200 trees is a point where accuracy usually plateaus while training stays within a minute or two on ~54,000 rows; other settings default (unbounded depth, `max_features="sqrt"`).
- `SGDClassifier(loss="log_loss", penalty="l2", alpha=1e-4, max_iter=1000, tol=1e-3, random_state=42)`: a logistic model trained by SGD, needed because Step 7 uses `partial_fit` (LogisticRegression and RandomForest have none). No `class_weight`: sklearn rejects `class_weight="balanced"` in `partial_fit`, and the data is balanced per year. `alpha=1e-4` is the sklearn default and a standard regularisation level for ~50k samples. For `partial_fit` the first call passes `classes=[0, 1]`.

**Report.** `docs/step4_models.md`: the three models, why each, the hyperparameter table and justification, training time per model, any convergence warnings, and tuning results if run.

**Testing.** Synthetic separable data: each model trains and predicts both classes with accuracy above chance (e.g. > 0.9); `build_model` returns the right class with `random_state == 42` (and `class_weight == "balanced"` for logreg only, `n_estimators == 200` where applicable); unknown name raises; the model returned by `build_model("sgd")` can be fit and then called with `partial_fit(X, y)` without error (not just "has the method"); same seed gives identical predictions twice; training with rows from a test year raises (guard checked via `years_train` argument in `train_all_from_split`, see below). A test that the training matrix has only years 2014-2016, and that `train_all_from_split` raises on a split containing a test year.

---

## Steps 5 and 6: Evaluation (`src/evaluate.py`)

**Approach.** Predict on held-out test years 2017-2021 only. Malware (1) is the positive class. Step 5 is the pooled table; Step 6 is the per-year breakdown.

**Functions.**
- `compute_metrics(y_true: np.ndarray, y_pred: np.ndarray) -> dict[str, float]`: `accuracy, precision, recall, f1`, using `pos_label=1`, `zero_division=0`.
- `evaluate_model(model, X_test, y_test) -> dict[str, float]`.
- `pooled_table(models: dict, X_test, y_test) -> pd.DataFrame`: one row per classifier, columns `model, accuracy, precision, recall, f1, n_test` (Step 5; pooled over 2017-2021).
- `per_year_table(models: dict, X_test, y_test, years_test) -> pd.DataFrame`: one row per (model, year), same metrics plus `year, n`; only years in `TEST_YEARS` (Step 6).
- `drift_summary(per_year: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame`: per model: first-test-year F1, last-test-year F1, drop, and the F1 slope across years.
- `assert_test_years_only(years: np.ndarray) -> None`: raises if any year is outside `TEST_YEARS`.
- `sensitivity_tables(models: dict, X_test, y_test, years_test, dup_mask: np.ndarray) -> tuple[pd.DataFrame, pd.DataFrame]`: the same pooled and per-year tables restricted to test rows where `dup_mask` is False (no exact duplicate in 2014-2016), with a `n_excluded` column; `dup_mask` comes from `train_duplicate_mask` (Step 1). Saved as `results/step5_pooled_no_dup.*` and `results/step6_per_year_no_dup.*`.
- `save_table(df: pd.DataFrame, stem: str) -> None`: writes `results/<stem>.csv` and `results/<stem>.md` (Markdown table with fixed rounding to 4 decimals).
- Entry point for Steps 5 (and later 6): `main.run_step5(df=None, split=None, models=None) -> dict[str, pd.DataFrame]`, consistent with `run_step1` to `run_step4` (the earlier `run_evaluation(df)` was not built). It reuses the Step 4 models when given, otherwise trains them on 2014-2016; writes `results/step5_metrics.*` (with a `baseline_accuracy` column), `results/step5_confusion.*` and `results/step5_pooled_no_dup.*`. Step 6 is `main.run_step6(df=None, split=None, models=None)` (same pattern; reuses the Step 4 models, never refits on a test year). It writes `results/step6_by_year.*` (columns `classifier, year, n, accuracy, precision, recall, f1`; `by_year_export` renames `model` to `classifier`), `results/step6_baseline_by_year.*` (`year_baseline_table`: n, class counts, majority-class accuracy per year), `results/step6_drift_summary.*` (`drift_summary`), `results/step6_per_year_no_dup.*` and the figure `results/step6_by_year.png` (`plot_by_year`; F1 and accuracy by year; replaces the planned name `step6_f1_by_year.png` as the lead engineer asked).

**Notes.** Pooled metrics weight years by size (2017-2018 are 6x larger than 2019-2021), so the per-year table is the primary view; the report says so.

**Reports.** `docs/step5_evaluation.md` (pooled table, accuracy as the primary metric, plus precision/recall/F1 and a short comparison). `docs/step6_test_results.md` (per-year table for each classifier, how performance changes as data drifts, link to Step 2 findings).

**Testing.** Hand-computed confusion matrix (e.g. TP=3, FP=1, FN=2, TN=4) gives the exact accuracy, precision, recall and F1; metrics treat 1 as positive (swapping labels changes precision/recall); all-benign predictions give recall 0 and precision 0 without raising; `per_year_table` has one row per model per test year, the row counts `n` sum to the pooled `n_test`, and weighted per-year accuracy equals the pooled accuracy; `assert_test_years_only` raises on a training year; files are written with the expected columns. `train_duplicate_mask` flags a hand-built test row identical to a training row and not a unique one; `sensitivity_tables` excludes exactly the flagged rows and `n + n_excluded` equals the full test count.

---

## Step 7: Sustainable approach (`src/sustainable.py`)

**Approach.** Compare four strategies on the same test years (2017-2021), same metrics (accuracy, precision, recall, F1; malware positive), reported per year and pooled. Rule for all of them: year t is predicted before any of its rows is used for training or for fitting preprocessing.

| Strategy | Training data used to predict year t |
|---|---|
| (a) static | 2014-2016 only, never updated (this is the Step 4/6 model) |
| (b) expanding window | all years before t (2014..t-1); preprocessing and model refit from scratch for each t |
| (c) sliding window | the 3 years before t (t-3..t-1); preprocessing and model refit for each t |
| (d) incremental | SGD fit on 2014-2016, then for t = 2017..2021: predict t, then `partial_fit` on t (test-then-train) |

For t=2017 the windows in (b) and (c) are both 2014-2016, so (a)-(c) agree on 2017; they differ from 2018 on.

**Functions.**
- Step 7 guard: every Step 7 fit goes through `window_years` (which raises if any returned year is >= t) and then `check_no_overlap(window, [t])`. `train_all_from_split` is not used here.
- `window_years(strategy: str, t: int) -> tuple[int, ...]`: training years for strategy `"static"`, `"expanding"` or `"sliding"` at test year t (static: 2014-2016; expanding: 2014..t-1; sliding: t-3..t-1); raises if t is not in `TEST_YEARS` or if any returned year is >= t.
- `run_window_strategy(df, strategy: str, model_name: str = "logreg") -> pd.DataFrame`: for each t: `check_no_overlap(window, [t])`, fit a new `Preprocessor` and model on the window only, predict t, compute metrics; returns one row per test year.
- `run_incremental(df, model_name: str = "sgd") -> pd.DataFrame`: initial `fit` of `Preprocessor` and SGD on 2014-2016 (preprocessor frozen afterwards, so later years use the same mask and scaler: a limitation noted in the report); loop over t, record the prediction on t first, then `partial_fit` on year t with the true labels. Returns one row per test year.
- `run_all_strategies(df, split=None, models=None, step4_seconds=None, rf=True) -> pd.DataFrame`: concatenates (a)-(d) with `strategy` and `classifier` columns, one row per (strategy, classifier, test year); static rows come from the Step 4 models when given. **Changed in Step 7:** the pooled rows are not in this table (a `year` column stays numeric); `pooled_by_strategy` writes them separately.
- `compare_to_static(results: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame`: per strategy and year, difference in F1 and accuracy against the static model.
- `run_sustainable(df, split=None, models=None, step4_seconds=None, rf=True) -> dict[str, pd.DataFrame]`: writes `results/step7_strategies.*` (columns `strategy, classifier, year, n, accuracy, precision, recall, f1`; replaces the planned name `step7_strategy_metrics`, as the lead engineer asked), `step7_strategies_detail.*` (adds confusion counts, training seconds, rows and window), `step7_pooled.*`, `step7_vs_static.*`, `step7_summary.*` (mean F1, worst year), `step7_cost.*`, `step7_window_composition.*` and `step7_f1_by_year.png` (F1 and accuracy by year, dashed always-malware F1 0.667 and chance accuracy 0.5).
- Helpers: `year_arrays`, `fit_on_years` (the single place every window fit goes through: `check_no_overlap` plus a `max(years) < t` assertion), `static_from_models`, `pooled_by_strategy`, `summary_table`, `cost_table`, `window_composition`, `plot_strategies`. `run_incremental` also asserts before every prediction that no year seen so far is >= t.

**Model choice and decision flagged.** Windows (b)-(c) and the static baseline use LogisticRegression so that all five refits finish in a few minutes; (d) uses SGD. A fair isolation of "incremental vs retrain" would also run SGD under (a)-(c); I will add SGD-static as an extra row (cheap) so the incremental gain is compared with the same model family. RandomForest is run for (a) and (b) only (not (c) or (d)); measured, it fit within the budget. Runtime estimate: ~54,000-90,000 rows x ~1,000 features per LR refit, 5 refits per strategy; to be measured, not assumed.

**Assumption to state.** Labels for year t become available only after year t ends (test-then-train); a real labeling delay would hurt (d), (b) and (c) in practice. The report states this. Not simulated here.

**Row-count imbalance (to state in the report).** Years 2014-2018 have 18,000 rows each and 2019-2021 have 3,000, so the expanding window is dominated by old data and the 3-year window for 2021 (2018-2020) is 18,000 of 24,000 rows from 2018. The report notes that "retraining helps or not" may partly reflect this row-count imbalance rather than recency alone, and lists each window's year composition (rows per year in the training window for every strategy and test year; also saved as `results/step7_window_composition.csv`). No equal-rows variant is run.

**Report.** `docs/step7_sustainable_approach.md`: the four strategies, the table of F1/accuracy per year, the window composition table and the imbalance note above, comparison with the static model, cost (training time per strategy), conclusions that feed the one-page report.

**Testing.** Synthetic multi-year frame with an injected drift (class boundary shifts each year): `window_years` returns exactly the specified years (including edge cases t=2017 and t=2021); for every strategy and every t, `max(window) < t` (the no-test-year-in-training check, run through a spy that records the years passed to `fit`); `run_incremental` records predictions on t before `partial_fit` on t (verified with a stub model that logs call order and, separately, by checking the year-t labels are not seen at prediction time); static results are identical to the Step 6 model's results; result tables have one row per test year per strategy and the expected columns; on the injected-drift data the retraining/incremental strategies do not do worse than the static one in the final year (sanity check, not a performance claim).

---

## Cross-cutting test plan (tester)
- `tests/test_stepN_*.py` per step with synthetic data in `tmp_path`; real-data tests marked and skipped when `input_data/` is absent.
- A project-wide leakage test: every call that fits anything records the years it saw (via a spy/wrapper); none of 2017-2021 may appear before its own prediction. Applies to Steps 3-7; `drift.py` (Step 2) is exempt.
- `python harness.py test N` for one step and `python harness.py test all` for all.

## Implementation order and commits
One commit per task (about 300 added lines max): config + data, then drift, then preprocess, then models, then evaluate, then sustainable, then main and docs. Each step is followed by a review and test cycle outside this plan.

## Points where I disagree or want a decision
1. The accuracy matrix in Step 2 trains on later years and predicts earlier ones; this is a diagnostic only, not used for any design choice, and is exempt from the leakage rules (section 0).
2. Step 7 (d) freezes the scaler and zero-column mask from 2014-2016; an alternative (updating the scaler with `partial_fit`) is possible but not planned.
3. Cross-year duplicates (item 5 above) stay in the main results; the sensitivity row reports the effect.
